title: What If a Neutron Star Passed Through the Solar System?
description:
A new what-if every day at 5:48 pm (Riyadh).

A neutron star is what is left when a giant star collapses: about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun crushed into a ball roughly 20 km across, the size of a city. It is so dense that a teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes, and the fastest known one spins 716 times every second. If one drifted through the solar system it would not need to hit anything: its gravity alone, stronger than the Sun's, could pull the planets off their orbits and fling Earth into deep space. Most neutron stars are small and faint, so spotting one heading our way would be hard.

Sources: NASA Imagine the Universe, neutron stars (about 1.4 solar masses, about 20 km across); Hessels et al., Science (2006), PSR J1748-2446ad spinning 716 times per second.
Narration is AI-generated (ElevenLabs) and the pictures and opening clip are AI-generated. This is a thought experiment.
